turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Got your vitals before the doctor steps in. Blood pressure is one eighteen over seventy four, heart rate one oh six, respirations twenty four, oxygen sat ninety four percent, temperature thirty seven point one.
[SEG0002] person_1 (NURSE): Peak flow, I first wrote three hundred and fifty, no, looking again it's three hundred and twenty. Chart says your best was four hundred and eighty.
[SEG0003] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I just sit? I'm wiped out. That waiting-room TV is awful.
[SEG0004] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dr. Shah. What brought you in?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't breathe right. I'm wheezing. It came on after a cold.
[SEG0006] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his mom, Priya. It's been three weeks of this, and he downplays everything.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It has not been three weeks. The wheeze is like five days. Let me talk.
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wheeze for five days, or three weeks?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days.
[SEG0010] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cough and that whistle have been about three weeks. I live with him, I hear it.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): So five days to three weeks. When did the cold start?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't date it. Since Diwali or after, I don't know. Last winter, or the one before, that was some other mess, not this.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bringing anything up with the cough?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): I have a cough. It's dry. No gunk.
[SEG0019] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He wakes up wheezing at night. I've heard it the past few nights.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I do not wake up wheezing. I sleep. I'm just tired during the day. Stop.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath sitting still?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not sitting. When I walk. I can still get a sentence out, it's just annoying.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Inhalers?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): The blue one. I was hitting it every hour, no, not every hour. Maybe five, six times a day. Two puffs.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): That blue one is albuterol, the rescue?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I think. I mix it up with the brown one. Half the time I don't know which is which.
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The brown one is fluticasone. The box says one hundred and ten micrograms, no, two hundred and twenty. He's supposed to take two puffs twice a day.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I do one puff, when I even use it. Mostly it sits in the drawer. Sometimes I grab the brown one for the wheeze and leave the blue. I honestly don't know.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): So you're not sure you take the fluticasone the way it was prescribed.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. I don't know.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any other meds?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0035] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does. Penicillin gave him a rash when he was little. I remember it.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember that. I don't have allergies.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Asthma history?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Since I was seven, no, since I was ten. No surgeries.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0041] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad has asthma. He lives with me. He's in community college and he's barely working this semester.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me listen to your lungs.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Wheeze in both lungs. No crackles. Mild pulling in under the ribs. You're still moving air.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Cool. Are we done? I'm tired of this.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): This is an asthma flare after that cold. That's what I'm treating.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Just give me something that works.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Prednisone by mouth, fifty milligrams, no, forty milligrams, once a day for five days.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days. Whatever.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blue albuterol stays two puffs for symptoms. If you need it more than every four hours, call or go in.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Brown is the preventer, fluticasone, not the rescue. Blue is the rescue. Don't swap them.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, okay.
[SEG0052] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he uses the right one. The parking meter outside is probably expired, whatever, I'll deal with it.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): If this hasn't settled in two days, we might get a chest x-ray. Not today.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come back to clinic in three days for a recheck.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days? Seriously?
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. If you worsen tonight, hard to talk, lips turning blue, go to the ER.
[SEG0057] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get him there if that happens.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm nineteen. I can get myself there.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): Questions on the prednisone?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Is it gonna mess up my sleep? I'm already not sleeping... no, I sleep. I'm just tired. Forget I said that.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): It can make you jittery. Take it in the morning with food.
[SEG0062] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the prednisone instructions and walk you up front.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): Finally.

clinical_uncertainties.description: The patient cannot date when the cold started, saying only that it was since Diwali or after.
The mother says the cough and wheeze have lasted about three weeks, while the patient says the wheeze has lasted five days.
The mother reports nighttime wheezing over the past few nights, and the patient denies waking up wheezing.
The mother said fluticasone is 220 micrograms and supposed to be two puffs twice a day, while the patient said he uses one puff when he uses it, so the puff count is not a single agreed dose.

The patient is not sure he takes fluticasone as prescribed: he takes one puff when he uses it, it mostly sits in the drawer, and he sometimes uses the brown inhaler for wheeze and leaves the blue one.
The patient denies any drug allergy, while his mother recalls a childhood rash from penicillin.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
